The leaf-eared mouse Phyllotis darwini, a sigmodontine rodent endemic to the semi-arid and Mediterranean ecosystems of Chile, displays life-history traits shaped by the region's pronounced seasonal variability in resource availability. In captive colonies maintained at a constant core temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a value that approximates the species' typical thermoneutral zone, gestation has been documented to last exactly 18 days [tg = 18 days], a period that is relatively short even among small-bodied sigmodontines. This abbreviated gestation is followed by the birth of altricial neonates; the wet weight at birth of these newborns is approximately 3 grams [Wwb = approximately 3 grams], a remarkably modest mass that necessitates a prolonged period of maternal investment. The pups are born with closed eyes and limited locomotor ability, entirely dependent on the mother's milk for their early development. The rapid completion of the gestational phase is ecologically advantageous, permitting females to capitalize on brief pulses of food availability, which are typical of the unpredictable winter rainfall that defines their habitat.

The post-natal developmental trajectory of Phyllotis darwini is marked by several key milestones that occur under these same thermally stable conditions. Females reach puberty at 57 days after birth [tp = 57 days after birth] when maintained at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], an age that underscores a relatively fast maturation rate for a rodent of its ultimate size. This early onset of reproductive capability is balanced, however, by the substantial energetic demands of lactation and pup rearing. Weaning, marking the cessation of milk dependence and the transition to an adult diet of seeds and herbaceous matter, occurs at 34 days after birth [tx = 34 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. The interval between weaning and pubertal onset thus spans approximately 23 days, during which the young must achieve sufficient somatic growth and fat reserves to survive the coming dry season. This developmental schedule aligns with the seasonal peak in primary productivity, ensuring that weanlings encounter abundant food resources as they learn to forage independently.

In terms of adult body size, field-collected specimens and captive-bred individuals indicate that the species attains an ultimate wet weight of 50.8 grams [Wwi = 50.8 grams] under optimal conditions. This modest mass, typical of small omnivorous murids, is correlated with a relatively high surface-area-to-volume ratio, necessitating the elevated metabolic rates observed at the species' preferred ambient temperatures. The maximum lifespan under controlled captive conditions is 4 years [am = 4 years] when animals are housed at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a longevity that is considerable for a rodent of this size and suggests a life-history strategy that balances high reproductive output against a moderate risk of extrinsic mortality. In the wild, predation by owls and foxes likely truncates this potential considerably, selecting for early and intense reproductive effort. The trade-off between maintaining somatic condition and achieving reproductive success is thus a central axis of its life-history evolution.

Reproductive output in Phyllotis darwini is characterized by a high potential for rapid population growth. Females produce litters of up to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = up to 4 pups per litter] under favorable conditions, reflecting a capacity for substantial per-event fecundity. Furthermore, under the stable thermal regime of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the estimated birthing frequency is approximately one litter every two years [F_R_i = approximately one litter every two years], a rate that translates into a potential annual reproductive output of about 2 pups per year. This combination of moderate litter size and low litter frequency allows the species to slowly build populations even during resource-poor periods. The reproductive rate is thus tightly coupled to environmental stochasticity, with females capable of initiating consecutive pregnancies shortly after parturition under favorable resource conditions.

Comparative analyses with congeneric species from more stable, mesic environments further illuminate the ecological specialization of Phyllotis darwini. The relatively short gestation of 18 days [tg = 18 days] and the brief time to weaning, which occurs at 34 days after birth [tx = 34 days after birth], both observed at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], contrast with the slower developmental pace of Phyllotis magister, which inhabits higher-elevation, more predictable Andean habitats. Similarly, the early pubertal age of 57 days after birth [tp = 57 days after birth] and the ultimate wet weight of 50.8 grams [Wwi = 50.8 grams] align with predictions from r-selection theory for species occupying fluctuating environments at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. The maximum lifespan of 4 years [am = 4 years], though modest on an absolute scale, represents a significant investment in somatic persistence relative to its small body mass at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This suite of traits positions P. darwini as a classic example of an opportunistic, fast-living strategist adapted to the profound climatic variability of the Chilean matorral.
